results.name: arithmetic_relation_target_excess
results.description: Yes rate for non-example targets equal to the sum or difference of two examples minus the yes rate of other non-example targets in the same sets (sets with 2+ examples); observed > null means people use arithmetic relations between examples that the model's concepts lack.

results.name: offrule_residue_class_contrast
results.description: Among sets of 3+ examples whose pairwise differences share a gcd d >= 4 (d != 10) but which are not multiples of d (e.g. 33,17,5,9 = 1 mod 4), yes rate for non-example targets in the same residue class mod d minus targets outside it; observed > null means people detect "same remainder" regularities the model has no concept for.

results.name: between_set_yes_variance
results.description: Variance across sets (with >= 10 trials) of the set-level yes rate; observed > null means people's breadth of generalisation differs between sets more than the model predicts (some sets far broader/narrower), observed < null means the model makes set breadths too heterogeneous.

results.name: order_permuted_set_gap
results.description: Mean absolute difference in yes rate, on shared targets, between sets containing the same numbers shown in a different order (e.g. "16,8" vs "8,16"); the model is order-invariant, so observed > null means presentation order changes people's generalisation beyond sampling noise.
results.code:
# name: order_permuted_set_gap
# description: Mean absolute difference in yes rate, on shared targets, between sets containing the same numbers shown in a different order (e.g. "16,8" vs "8,16"); the model is order-invariant, so observed > null means presentation order changes people's generalisation beyond sampling noise.
def test_statistic(df):
    d = df[["number_set", "target", "rating"]].copy()
    sets = d["number_set"].unique()
    key = {s: ",".join(sorted(s.split(","), key=int)) for s in sets}
    d["key"] = d["number_set"].map(key)
    m = d.groupby(["key", "number_set", "target"])["rating"].mean().reset_index()
    n_orders = m.groupby(["key", "target"])["number_set"].transform("nunique")
    m = m[n_orders >= 2]
    if len(m) == 0:
        return 0.0
    rng = m.groupby(["key", "target"])["rating"].agg(lambda x: x.max() - x.min())
    return float(rng.mean())

results.name: digit_reversal_target_excess
results.description: Yes rate for targets that are the digit reversal of an example (e.g. 13 -> 31) minus the yes rate of other non-example targets in the same sets; observed > null means people generalise to digit-reversed numbers more than the model's rule/interval concepts predict.

results.name: prime_set_prime_vs_odd_composite
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that are all odd primes, yes rate for prime targets minus odd composite targets (non-examples); observed > null means people pick out "primes" over "odd numbers" more sharply than the model, observed < null means the model over-commits to the primes rule.

results.name: shared_nonlast_digit_contrast
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that share a common digit but not a common last digit (e.g. 13,91 share 1), yes rate for non-example targets containing a shared digit minus targets containing none; observed > null means people lean on "contains digit" similarity more than the model, observed < null means the model over-uses contains-digit rules.

results.name: small_rule_hull_exception_yes
results.description: Among sets of 2+ examples that all fall in one small rule (<= 12 members: squares, cubes, powers of k, multiples of 9/11/12), yes rate for non-rule targets lying inside the examples' range; observed > null means people fill in the numeric range around tight-rule sets more than the model (its size principle is too sharp), observed < null means less.
